<div class="rs-intro">
  <div class="rs-lede">
    <p>I build optimization and techno-economic models for decisions about low-carbon energy systems: what to build, where, how to run it, and under which market and policy conditions it pays off.</p>
    <p>My doctoral research asked one question at three scales: when does flexibility, from hydrogen or from demand, add value to a low-carbon energy system? The answer at the national scale raised the question behind my current work: what can carry the capital cost of new firm, low-carbon supply, now that AI data centers need hundreds of megawatts around the clock?</p>
    <p>Each project page shows the problem, the hard parts, the design choices and the findings with their limits.</p>

<!-- ============ chapter 1: flexibility from plant to nation (Ph.D.) ============ -->
<section class="chapter theme-hydrogen" id="flexibility" aria-labelledby="h-flex">
  <div class="ch-head">
    <span class="ch-num">Chapter 1 · Ph.D., The University of Texas at Dallas, and Idaho National Laboratory</span>
    <h2 id="h-flex" class="rs-h2">Flexibility from plant to nation</h2>
    <p>One question at three scales: when does flexibility, from hydrogen or from demand, add value to a low-carbon energy system? Each step up in scale changed who makes the decision, which uncertainty matters most, and where flexibility gets its value.</p>
  </div>
  <ol class="steps">
    <li class="step">
      <span class="step-scale">Plant</span>
      <h3>Hydrogen makes wind output firmer and more valuable</h3>
      <p>I extended an open optimization model with electrolysis, hydrogen storage and fuel cells, and co-optimized equipment sizes with hourly operation for a wind farm, then for solar and offshore wind plants. Two of the studies showed that the cost per kilogram of hydrogen and the cost of the whole system can move in opposite directions. These models took the site as given, so they could not say where to build across a region.</p>
      <p class="step-links"><a href="projects/wind-hydrogen.html">Wind–hydrogen</a><a href="projects/solar-hydrogen.html">Solar–hydrogen</a><a href="projects/offshore-wind-hydrogen-om.html">Offshore O&amp;M</a></p>
    </li>
    <li class="step">
      <span class="step-scale">State</span>
      <h3>Coordinating hydrogen supply and demand under uncertainty</h3>
      <p>For Texas, I built the inputs from public market disclosures and a two-stage stochastic model that sizes hydrogen assets in eight weather zones and schedules them hour by hour across scenarios of demand and renewable build-out. The model showed how the price of gas-fired backup power changes where green hydrogen goes.</p>
      <p class="step-links"><a href="projects/txh2.html">Texas hydrogen</a></p>
    </li>
    <li class="step">
      <span class="step-scale">National fleet</span>
      <h3>Making firm low-carbon supply flexible</h3>
      <p>During my internship at Idaho National Laboratory, I co-developed an hourly model that splits a reactor's output among grid sales, high-temperature electrolysis, storage and reserves, linked to a lifetime cash-flow analysis of 42 reactors in seven U.S. markets. Operated as baseload-only plants at 2024 prices, nearly all had negative net present value; with hydrogen integration, including the assumed hydrogen production credit, a majority reached positive net present value.</p>
      <p class="step-links"><a href="projects/npph2.html">Nuclear–hydrogen</a></p>
    </li>
  </ol>
</section>

<!-- ============ turning point ============ -->
<div class="turn" role="note" aria-labelledby="h-turn">  <!-- a div: Quarto moves aside elements into the margin -->
  <span class="turn-icon" aria-hidden="true"><i class="bi bi-signpost-split"></i></span>
  <div>
    <h2 id="h-turn" class="turn-title">The question that led to data centers</h2>
    <p>The fleet study showed that hydrogen, with the assumed production credit, and grid services can change the economics of existing reactors, while new reactors depend on capital cost and policy support. What could carry the capital cost of new firm, low-carbon supply? Large AI data centers, which need hundreds of megawatts around the clock, often where the grid cannot connect them for years, made that question concrete.</p>
  </div>
</div>

<!-- ============ chapter 2: firm low-carbon power for AI data centers (current) ============ -->
<section class="chapter theme-datacenter" id="data-centers" aria-labelledby="h-dc">
  <div class="ch-head">
    <span class="ch-num">Chapter 2 · Research Associate, The University of Texas at Dallas; Postdoctoral Fellow, Kansas State University</span>
    <h2 id="h-dc" class="rs-h2">Firm low-carbon power for AI data centers</h2>
    <p>Small modular reactors can supply firm power at the scale of an AI campus. I study when such supply can compete with the alternatives, at the scale of one campus and of the United States.</p>
  </div>
  <ol class="steps">
    <li class="step">
      <span class="step-scale">Framing</span>
      <h3>What a credible assessment must capture</h3>
      <p>In a co-first-authored Perspective, I wrote the techno-economic analysis: reliability requirements, wide first-of-a-kind cost ranges, service-based metrics and co-products such as heat all change the comparison.</p>
      <p class="step-links"><a href="projects/smr-dc.html">SMR perspective</a></p>
    </li>
    <li class="step">
      <span class="step-scale">One campus</span>
      <h3>Where SMR cogeneration becomes competitive</h3>
      <p>For a hyperscale campus in Texas, I co-optimized reactor output, turbine steam extraction for absorption cooling and grid exchange, hour by hour. Capital cost and policy set the competitiveness boundary far more than operating choices do, and an output-based credit discourages using steam for cooling. <span class="status">Accepted in <em>Energy Conversion and Management</em>.</span></p>
      <p class="step-links"><a href="projects/nuclear-dc.html">SMR cogeneration</a></p>
    </li>
    <li class="step">
      <span class="step-scale">United States</span>
      <h3>Data-center demand and SMR commercialization</h3>
      <p>A national study asks whether data-center demand can help small modular reactors move from their first units to wider commercial deployment. <span class="status">Manuscript in preparation.</span></p>
      <p class="step-links"><a href="projects/smr-dc-national.html">Upcoming study</a></p>
    </li>
  </ol>

  <div class="sei" id="sei">
    <div class="sei-head">
      <span class="label">Proposal · Co-PI · under review (2026)</span>
      <h3>Secure power for Kansas data centers</h3>
      <p class="sei-src">Kansas State University Secure Energy Initiative, seed funding</p>
    </div>
    <p>Kansas is seeing data-center proposals of several hundred megawatts. The proposal asks how small modular reactors, their recoverable heat, data-center cooling and grid connections can be planned together, so that computing and cooling continue through disruptions at a cost the region can bear, with community priorities in siting and design.</p>
    <ol class="sei-modules" aria-label="Four research modules">
      <li><strong>Community and policy</strong> preferences and local conditions</li>
      <li><strong>Physical models</strong> of reactor heat, cooling and data-center operation</li>
      <li><strong>Integrated planning</strong> of locations, capacities and timing under uncertainty</li>
      <li><strong>Kansas demonstration</strong> at county level, with stakeholder review</li>
    </ol>
    <p class="sei-role"><strong>My role:</strong> coupled models, optimization, economics and software, in an interdisciplinary team spanning electrical, nuclear and civil engineering, water research and political science.</p>
  </div>
</section>

  <h2 id="h-support" class="rs-h2">Supporting capabilities</h2>

      <h3><span class="cdot"></span>Carbon signals and demand</h3>
      <p>Re-timing electricity use with hourly emission intensity across U.S. regions, and what that accounting can and cannot show.</p>
      <a href="projects/ghg.html">Emission-informed load regulation</a>
    </li>
    <li class="support-item theme-wind">
      <h3><span class="cdot"></span>Uncertainty quantification</h3>
      <p>Multi-fidelity Gaussian processes that combine the turbine's theoretical power curve with scarce measurements for probabilistic wind power.</p>
      <a href="projects/uq-mfgpr.html">Wind power curves</a>
      <a href="projects/national-wind-uq.html">Plant-level wind uncertainty</a>
    </li>
    <li class="support-item theme-datacenter">
      <h3><span class="cdot"></span>Interconnection economics</h3>
      <p>What waiting for grid energization costs a data-center developer, other ratepayers and society, and how staging recovers part of it.</p>
      <a href="projects/data-center-delay-economics.html">Cost of delayed energization</a>
    </li>
  </ul>
</section>
